title: Benny the Bat and the Moonbeam Mishap
markdown:
Benny the Bat was not a fan of the dark. Especially not the dark of the big creaky barn loft. Wind went past the boards and Benny pulled his leathery wings tighter, a hug he gave himself. A spiderweb tickled his nose—harmless, floaty—and he still squeaked. The loft held shadowy corners and mysterious bumps, the kind that sounded as if they might have legs. Benny preferred his cozy nook behind the dusty hay bales, where moonlight only peeked in like a shy spotlight. Whiskers did a wiggly dance. Heart went thump-thump-thump.

One evening, as he was getting ready for his usual hide-and-seek with the shadows (he was always It), a tiny sparkle zipped past his nose. Not a moth. A proper sparkly thing, with tinkly laughter like tiny bells dipped in honey, and a voice as bright as a buttercup.

“Benny! Benny the Bat! Are you there?”

He squeezed his eyes shut, which he figured was the best way to become invisible. “Go away, spooky shadow-thing. I’m not here. I’m a hay bale.”

The sparkle hovered closer. Dust motes danced. “Spooky? I’m Hazel. Hazel the Harvest Fairy. And I need your help.”

Benny peeked one eye. Hazel was small and bright, wings like crunchy autumn leaves, rustling swish-swish. She held a tiny shimmering parcel tied with gossamer thread so thin it looked like a captured moonbeam. It pulsed with silvery light, a tiny heartbeat of moonlight.

“Help?” His voice wobbled. “With what?”

“A moonbeam delivery. The moonbeams have been extra sparkly, and Farmer McGregor’s prize-winning pumpkins are droopy. They need extra moonlight magic before the harvest festival tomorrow. They’re practically sighing.”

Benny’s fur stood on end. “Moonbeams? In the dark? In the loft?” He burrowed deeper. “Too many things. Spiky things. Floaty things. Things that go boo.”

Hazel tilted her head. Leafy wings shimmered. “But Benny, you’re a bat. You live in the dark. You can see perfectly well.”

“That’s a myth. I see, yes, but mostly not-seeing. Feeling my way. The loft is a thousand dark places rolled into one giant bumpy whispery dark place. Dust bunnies the size of my head.”

Hazel sighed, cornstalks in a breeze. “Please. The pumpkins will be so sad. I’ve promised them the best moonbeams this side of the farm. They’re counting on us.” She held out the parcel. “I’ll be right here. Every flutter. I’ll even sing a happy song.”

Benny looked at her earnest face and the hopeful glow. He could not say no to Hazel. She made scary things a little less so. “Okay. I’ll try. But no singing too loud.”

So Benny, Hazel perched on his head like a tiny glowing hat, set off toward the dark yawning entrance of the loft. Up they flew. Heart thump-thump-thump, a drum solo. The parcel wobbled in her tiny hands. “Careful, Hazel.” His wings felt clumsy, as if a wind were there when it wasn’t. He imagined grumpy badger shadows and giggling owl shadows. The parcel wobbled like a tower of important blocks.

Suddenly a gust of wind, like a playful giant puffing its cheeks right into the barn, rushed through a broken pane of glass. The moonbeam parcel, with a little silvery swoosh, flew out of Hazel’s grasp and tumbled toward the darkest corner of the loft. “Oh no,” cried Hazel, a tiny gasp. Benny flapped wildly, eyes wide, fur doing the frantic dance again. The parcel, a tiny silver speck against the inky black, headed for a pile of old creaky farm equipment that probably had not moved since the last ice age. He could not see a thing. He blinked and flapped, but it was all just dark. This was it: the ultimate scary dark, the Everest of darkness.

Then his ears twitched. He did not see the dark. He heard it. The dusty thud of the parcel landing. Wind whispering through rafters. A faint drip-drip from a leaky roof, like tiny water-fairies tapping. And he remembered the clicks and squeaks he made to find his way. Echolocation. A secret map for the dark. Ears with flashlights.

“Wait.” His voice came clearer. “I can hear it.” Rapid clicks, a little bat-symphony. Sounds bounced back and painted the loft: rough beams, dusty sacks, forgotten tools. In his mind’s ear the parcel nestled near old sacks, safe. “Hazel. I know where it is.”

He zipped, clicks guiding like a secret map only he could read. Hazel clung, amazed and a little giggly. They swooped and swirled. He felt the bumpy floorboards beneath, the rough beams above, cool air currents tickling his wings. A stack of sacks appeared in sound before it appeared in sight. There it was, just as he had heard, a little dusty, as if it had taken a nap.

Then another gust, stronger than the last, a grumpy dragon sneeze that whoomphed through the barn. Benny’s wings flapped as if waving goodbye to someone invisible. He strained for the parcel. The wind snatched it deeper into the corner he had always avoided: rustling like whispering secrets, the smell of old forgotten things, maybe hats or long-lost socks. Bravery wobbled.

He was scared. Truly bat-scared. He looked at Hazel’s face, trust and a little worry, and thought of droopy pumpkins wilting toward tomorrow’s festival. He remembered the amazing feeling of hearing his way, the loft painted in bounce-back. A deep shaky breath, a little bellows. “Okay, Hazel. Hold on tight. This is it.” A mighty beat, straight into the deepest darkest part of the loft. He ignored the shadows, the rustling, the creepy almost-whispers. He focused on clicks: click-click-clack, mapping the dark with precision. He swooped and dodged, wings a determined rhythm, a tiny superhero on a delivery. In his mind: the gleam of the parcel caught on a forgotten rake like a sleeping giant’s comb. He took it gently in his claws. Heart a triumphant drum. He had flown into the middle of the thing he hated and come out holding the cargo. A happy little chirp.

Parcel tucked under his chin, they flew down. The loft felt less like dread and more like a job finished. The prize pumpkins still sagged. Hazel placed a piece of moonbeam on each. Instantly they puffed, orange skins glowing soft and cheerful, as if they had napped and drunk sunshine. They even seemed to wink.

Back in his favourite nook Benny watched as the moonlight, now delivered to the pumpkins, scattered little shimmering sparkles all over the barn loft. The loft was not a scary mysterious place anymore. It was just the loft: full of interesting sounds and shadows that now seemed playful, not frightening, hide-and-seek he no longer had to lose. He stretched his wings, a little tired, a big warm brave feeling in his chest like a friendly sunbeam swallowed. He was not afraid of the dark loft anymore. Not one bit. He had flown into it twice, heard his way, and brought the parcel home. He was Benny the Bat, the brave bat of the barn loft, and Hazel, still a little dusty, hummed very quietly after all.
